title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 1 (Part 2)  Application of CLO3D in Innovative Fashion Design Graduate Courses
description:
Dialogue with a teacher from the London College of Fashion: Exploring the application and learning of CLO3D in the innovative postgraduate fashion design course!

CLO3D software helps students master virtual garment design techniques and foster innovation. In their projects, students create custom fitting mini-programs to present VR filter effects of clothing online, achieving lifelike runway shows of classical costume restorations! Click the video to see more details!
transcript:
Okay Ella, we are very excited to hear more about your program and how CLO has been used.  
Now I'm handing it over to you, you can start whenever you are ready.  
Thank you very much.  

Okay, so hello everyone, I'm Ella Sharp, I'm the course leader for the MA Innovative Fashion Production course, which I'm sure you've had all the intros, but I've got it on my text so I'll do it again, LCF, which is part of the University of the Arts London.  
And thank you CLO3D for inviting me to talk to you today.  
I'm actually going to talk about how we use CLO in the MA IFP course, which is probably not the full range that many other people use, but we use it for very specific reasons.  
So, below you can see my contact details.  
I just want to explain, we use the wide range of functions in CLO3D, and it means that there are a variety of teams from buying and marketing to design and product development.  
And they all use the software differently, but they are interconnected.  
And on the MA IFP, we research into and develop strategies to connect their diversities.  
Thank you.  
And we have a really good relationship with the product development team.  
And I'm going to turn it over to you, CLO3D.  
Thank you.  
And I'm going to turn it over to you, CLO3D.  
And I'm going to turn it over to you, CLO3D.  

On this particular slide you can see a range of products and how we integrate them into tech packs and tracking documents and this work was a group project where students had to create a capsule collection for a brand extension where they shared the color and materials palettes and they made digital and physical samples. They also had to cost garments and think about how much they were going to put into production and balance the merchandising both from a brand to customer focus but also from a brand to the manufacturing phase.  

And in the following stuff that are essential in the prototyping and manufacturing of clothing. Now you can see here that we have moved away from using CADs, we're not using CADs anymore, we're moving directly into OBJ files. This is a bit of a hybrid. Sometimes we send OBJ files to the factory so they can actually look inside the garments to see how, for example, a facing might be stitched to the lining and we're working towards creating accurate digital samples which the factories can work from physically. So the idea being that factories can look inside the digital version and think oh that's how they want it made and make the garments.  

And when we're constructing digital samples in CLO3D we have to cut the patterns and sew them digitally differently to the physical assembling process. So this is complex and does require a strong understanding of physical construction methods to interrogate the accuracy of the digital sample otherwise the physical piece won't fit. So we have to be able to understand how to construct samples digitally and physically because when we make them we've got to consider the particle distance obviously and layering process to stop linings for example popping through the outer layer of the garments. Not something a conventional pattern cutter or design studio would have to think about, they'd have to think about it in the physical context but not necessarily from a drawing perspective. So when we're making we're thinking digitally and physically simultaneously.  

Our course focuses on all the information teams need to get a concept to the shop floor and end of life. And this is how the product can be, for example, repurposed or recycled. We really use CLO3D to help us visualize this. It's really important to us. The fashion industry really needs to change rapidly in response, we believe, to the decades of practice that's created a linear approach, disconnecting the manufacture and retailing apparel.  

At LCF, we are really aware that the climate crisis is here and that underpins all of our teaching and our understanding of how the fashion industry needs to innovate and evolve, but rapidly, and we've got to change the way we make and consume clothing. We need to reduce environmental impact. It's essential, not only in the physical production of clothing, but also in digital options.  

Sometimes we have virtual fashion, metaverse brands discussing or saying that virtual fashion is so much more sustainable than physical fashion. But there are a lot of different ways of doing that. And I think that's really important. There are a lot of energy and precious metals, and environmental impact, you know, with mining for precious metals, for battery, storing digital files. So it's not straightforward.  

But here I wanted to show you something that Jai has created. This is one of our recent graduates, she created a full-length coat, and her whole business model was to create a full-length coat and create a disassembly and reconstruction system into the range of garments. The business model is based on a take-back modular principle meaning that the customers send back their garments and the business model envisages the repurposing of the panels as the garments wear out.  

This is actually a really good version or a really good example of how Jai envisaged the Ellen MacArthur Foundation butterfly diagram and how she actually included it in her business model and the way that she disassembled garments. But before she disassembled them she designed them. Essential to this is the use of CLO3D to show the factories and the customers how the garments can be remade into new garments because people can't always visualize how something would look.  

We really, really enjoy this. It's quite challenging. I think sometimes they don't know what they're doing and they don't know what they're doing and the students find it a bit of a like oh my goodness we've done this it looks good visually and I'm saying yes but what does it look like inside? And here you can see Jai's business model and she's replaced some of the physical processes in the production amendment phases along the top. So if you look along the top you can see conventional bespoke sort of point of sale to delivery with the customer and on the bottom you can see how she's reimagined that using or integrating digital prototyping.  

And for this project Jai investigated bespoke clothing making on-demand and to an individual specification which CLO3D is well suited for. I have got her film, I've got three short clips of film at the end of this presentation showing you how our students use CLO3D within their master's projects. So if you're interested in learning more about the course you can click on the link in the description below.  

So here you can see her flow-throughs and also attention to avatar. So on our course we do a lot of work which investigates body scanning and avatar editing and the reason being that if we consider high street clothing, you know 30% of products don't sell and a lot of returns. The primary reason for returns is that they don't fit accurately. So we're really working hard at creating accurate avatars.  

And here you can see how Jai had investigated different ways of collecting data to create avatars. I mean all software programs have their limitations and for us some of the physical tailoring measurements are missing in the CLO3D avatar editor so we use body scans and import object files to check the accuracy of the final fit cross-referencing. We also have some conventional tailoring size charts with scanning points of measure and they do differ.  

So if you look at the two middle ones I suppose probably create virtual me and also CLO3D those points of measure often relate more to scanning data scanning systems than they do to conventional pattern cutting. We show our students what the differences are and how to overcome them, address body diversity to make sure that clothes fit all body shapes and it's a great tool to ensure inclusivity. We look at very curvy shapes, we think about people who are heavier on their thighs. What I would really like to see is different cup sizes—that's my plea to CLO3D—but at the moment it's a great way for us to test garments.  

And on this slide you can see how Jai investigated different scanning technologies before editing the CLO3D avatar. And next up this was the next stage so you can see how she imported an object file into CLO3D and then adapted the avatar. She merged the body scan and the object file with the avatar to adapt a working model to allow her to test the garment prior to the final digital fitting and this was to ensure that the trousers that she made for her customer were really accurate.  

I love this tool. I like the fact that you can also take object files into Mixamo and articulate them and move them around. It's a really great tool from a pattern cutting perspective. This is like digital to physical and this is where we're really focusing on our course. Students can investigate their own areas of research but we ensure that everybody can leave the course understanding digital to physical.  

And this is a typical challenge we face a lot of times with the article writing process in our course. So this is a common practice in our course. A lot of times the feedback we get is from your students and the most important thing is that we don't describe all the details of the project in the summary of the presentation. So that's not just so we want to plainly explain to you that it's not just the details of the project it's the quality of the work that it is, the type as they are in the industry.  

With smartphone technology, you know, these garments could be digitally tried on by customers and the lineups show the diversity of target customers too. So students have to consider the physical attributes of the population. So for example, on the top line you've got Sydney which is a more culturally diverse body type whereas on the bottom because it's more Korean they've gone for a more conventional body data. The students did investigate city body definitions, you know city body measurements to look at the difference in the balance of body types across the two cities.  

But some of our students are really interested in the metaverse and doing purely digital clothing for their Masters of Arts project and for their career as well and they're free to explore this developing fashion market. We've had students doing metaverse, using AI to generate digital fabric, and virtual fashion does have its place as you can see in some of the work shown in the presentation. However, all our students have to create digital samples and test them in the physical process for technical accuracy. It's a way to fully understand how clothes are constructed and how they function.  

This is a raincoat, which is from the Sydney lineup from the previous slide and you can see how she's taken the avatar out of the file so for example the factory could investigate the inside of the garment. Yaoyao had really focused on digital clothing before she came to us but was quite shocked when I said I know you're going to have to make a real garment. But we're looking, we're working towards replacing physical product development and sampling with digital alternatives because so much sampling is really wasted.  

And you know typically a brand will either work with a factory to produce a sample using specification sheets or send physical garments to the factory but then the garments have got to be made and then sent back to the brand to be signed off. So there's a huge amount of physical waste happening and not all the processes can be replaced, but we focus on creating accurate digital twins of the physical garments that you can see here before cutting fabric. And this is absolutely a work in progress but we haven't completely sorted it out yet.  

But this is what we're asking students to create: a garment that looks exactly the same on the inside as the physical garment right down to, for example, the size of facings and the ISO stitch specifications. This slide shows the digital parka above and the physical garment below and again this is the same piece from the previous slide. You can see that there are differences.  

I mean this pattern was developed in CLO3D, it wasn't cut physically and then imported to sew up. Sometimes our students work on the avatar, we work in 3D and cut our patterns and flatten them and do a hybrid 3D/2D pattern cutting method but this one I think she actually cut in 2D flow and then she sewed it up but she still used CLO3D to develop the pattern.  

And you can see there were issues with accuracy so the physical one on the right-hand side of the bottom, the hood's actually bigger than in the digital version. But this was the first time that Yaoyao had been required to match the digital to the physical accurately and cut the pattern in CLO3D. It also shows the importance of the accuracy of the physics of digital materials which we hadn't. This was very early in the course, which is pretty much the second term of when the course had been launched that we started work using CLO3D and it was very new to us and to the students.  

And in this slide you can sort of see that this is a sample she's evaluating. Yingxi is evaluating and amending the pocket details. We create first patterns using CLO3D, we do lay plans, we plot them to test the accuracy of the pattern cutting. But here you can see how we use 2D and 3D simultaneously.  

And it's really important. Sometimes it's easier to make an amendment in 2D and have it appear in 3D and sometimes you want to mark up on a 3D and then appear directly in the pattern and that's a great thing to be able to do because typically what you have to do when you're doing physical samples is you'll do the amendments on the physical piece on the mannequin or on the model and then you've got to transfer that information direct onto the pattern whereas this method means you can do it in 3D digitally and it translates onto the pattern.  

It's really great. I can draw all over my patterns and they will arrive in my 2D pattern so I can do a rough mark and then I can do my lines in 2D and it looks much more refined in 3D.  

And here you can see the lay plan. So Yingxi was looking at her lay plan and she was looking at the amount of fabric she got. So the first lay plan she got 2.5 meters, she'd obviously been very wasteful with her fabric lay and then in the second on the piece on the right-hand side you can see that she's actually saved half a meter. I mean personally I think we could have got it tighter but it's really good that she can see it straight off and also then it can be exported into the bill of materials.  

So we use the BOM tool as well and then we transfer that information into Zedonk which is an enterprise resource planning software and then we transfer that information into Zedonk which is an enterprise resource planning software or an ERP. It could also be translated, you know, transferred into a PLM or a product lifecycle management tool but that tends to be more at bigger scale. ERPs are much better for small scale which is why we teach those.  

And here you can see that the information would go to tech packs. We are very interested in using CLOSET but we haven't got that far yet. It's complicated but we can only deliver so much information to our students. They can only absorb so much information within the course because it's teaching them about product development, manufacturing, tracking documentation as well. So it is that in itself is difficult and then making sure that they can do it digitally is another thing.  

But you can see here that the lay plan enabled her to understand the rating.  

So next question, you know many of the masters projects currently use CLO3D to prototype and present the process of translating digital to physical fashion incorporating smartphone filters or websites. And I really wanted to show you this. It's Yaoyao's master's project from 2021. She reverse engineered some garments from the designer duo Marknell and created 3D filters of the garments for her phone app concept.  

The premise being that consumers can engage with the designers in the creation of their clothing and in the near future they could also be able to try on digital garments pretty much before we manufacture them. If you can get enough traction with your customers to digitally try on something before they order it as long as we've got the digital files in place and the production in place we can then start to do production on demand. You might think of something like Unspun who are now doing denim on the west coast of the States but then exporting their files to manufacturers in Turkey for bespoke garments.  

So on this slide this is sort of like a snapshot of Yaoyao's project and it was a collaboration as I said before with Marknell to translate specific garments from their Spring Summer 22 collection into 3D filters and Snapchat. Yaoyao graduated in 2021 and she's now the creative director for Alterspace.com, a digital fashion platform working with designers to represent their physical garments digitally.  

So really interesting project that's come out of this and actually backed by Farfetch last year and they got funding as a startup. And here you can see the process of creating digital twins of the physical pieces and then the 3D filters in Snapchat. As I said, Yaoyao reversed… so she started with the physical pieces, and then it required her to import the patterns from the designers, the avatar meshes from Lens Studio into CLO3D, adapt them using the avatar editor in CLO3D, create the digital garments, export the avatars and the garments into Mixamo to animate them or to rig them, and then back into Lens Studio.  

It's a complex process but it demonstrates how CLO3D can be integrated into a digital workflow. It's not just a software that needs to be entirely, everything needs to be done entirely in CLO3D. You can play around with it and use it in different software packages.  

This is a project from this year's graduation group. Our students have a range of levels of skills in CLO3D. Some are interested in the visual media aspect. Some want to experiment with mocap or motion capture software to bring their vision to life.  

Yiran Shan recreated historical costumes from the tomb of Huang Shen from the Song Dynasty and recreated historical and cultural backgrounds integrating 3D technology, such as CLO3D and Unity3D. And Yiran is class of '22. And here you can see how she integrated CLO3D into the wider historical project and into the workflow.  

And although this application is not strictly fashion, the application of the concept is highly relevant to the fashion industry. So the importance of understanding the physical properties and accurate garment construction enabled Yiran to understand the sophistication of Song Dynasty textile construction and choose the appropriate fabrics to recreate the garments.  

As of course, we discussed in depth the physics as well as the visual properties of digital materials. You know, if the physics of the fabric are not accurate, then the twirls and the patterns we create in CLO3D won't be either.  

And here Yiran discussed the structure of the physical fabrics before selecting digital counterparts, demonstrating her understanding of both the physical and digital fabric. So I've put a link. This is her Unity scenario. So she created all the scenes and then put the avatar, the motion capture, the clothing. She edited the avatar to the exact size and height of the lady that she was recreating whose day in the life of shoes was created. And you can, yeah you can see it here. And it was a really nice little clip of movement so Yiran did her own mocap and then she imported it in and made the piece.  

These are the students past and present or have literally just graduated.  

Good. Okay, fine. So I will show you some films. This is Shenshan and she had a project called Pocket Mobile Tailor. I'm a digital fashion designer and a problem solver. The fashion industry is entering the 4.0 era. Emerging technologies are bringing a lot of innovation to the field and are a great opportunity to change the environmental problems caused by current fashion production and consumption.  

Bespoke tailoring is a good example of sustainable fashion but there are many limitations to this sector. This project combined the latest cutting-edge technology with the traditional bespoke model and developed a sustainable, cost-effective platform that can implement remote bespoke and meet the needs of a wider range of customers.  

People can register for this platform in different roles. As you can see, the platform also serves as a community. Here customers can find the designer they are interested in and click on their profile.  

Customers will need to create an avatar that will do a virtual fitting for them. There are two options to choose from. If they are not too particular about their fit, they can choose one of the default avatars. Otherwise, customers will need to take two photos of their body as instructed. An artificial intelligence will generate a bespoke avatar for them. At the same time, they can start communicating these to the designer.  

The designer will draw sketches for the customer and create a virtual garment based on their bespoke avatar. They can keep communicating through text box all the time with high flexibility in design.  

Once virtual garments are finished, customers can approve it through three different ways. First is the 3D model, the second is AR, and the last one is video. After a customer is satisfied with the virtual garment, they can start designing the bespoke avatar. The physical garments will be made by manufacturers and delivered to the customer.  

During the communication process, the real-time estimated price changes with every decision making. The customer is required to pay a deposit before the designer works and a final payment when the physical garment is ready. The customer's rating of the service is vital for the designer to engage the next business.  

And by sharing their shopping experience with the community, customers have the opportunity to modify their design in a better way. The customers have the opportunity to become influencers, thus attracting more people to use this platform to start their own creative journey.  

This is going to be a wonderful platform for designers and payers to be freelancers, fashionistas to show their strong personalities, independent designers to make samples for the new season, and for small manufacturers to expand their business.  

This is also the practice for the industry 4.0 in the fashion field, which is conducted to a more sustainable development of this sector.

chunks.title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 1 (Part 2)  Application of CLO3D in Innovative Fashion Design Graduate Courses
chunks.content: ## Application of CLO3D in MA Innovative Fashion Production Course at LCF This section outlines how CLO3D is integrated into the MA Innovative Fashion Production (IFP) course at London College of Fashion (LCF), focusing on its use in digital garment prototyping, product development, and sustainability strategies. Ella Sharp, the course leader, explains that CLO3D is used in diverse ways across different teams including buying, marketing, design, and product development, all interconnected through the software. The course emphasizes research and strategy development to bridge these diverse uses. Students undertake group projects such as creating capsule collections for brand extensions, involving shared color and material palettes, digital and physical samples, garment costing, production planning, and merchandising balance from brand to customer and manufacturing phases. A key innovation is the transition from traditional CAD files to OBJ files for factory communication, allowing manufacturers to virtually inspect garment construction details (e.g., how facings are stitched to linings). The goal is to develop accurate digital samples that factories can directly use to produce physical garments. Digital garment construction in CLO3D requires understanding physical construction processes, as digital sewing and cutting differ from physical methods. Considerations include particle distance (the digital equivalent of seam allowance) and layering to prevent lining fabric from showing through outer layers. This dual digital-physical mindset is essential for accuracy. The course covers the entire lifecycle of a product—from concept to shop floor and end-of-life—highlighting the potential for repurposing and recycling garments using CLO3D visualization. This aligns with the fashion industry's urgent need to shift from a linear production model to a circular, sustainable approach. --- ## Sustainability and Circular Fashion Business Models Using CLO3D This section discusses CLO3D’s role in supporting sustainable and circular fashion design, with examples from student projects focused on garment disassembly, modularity, and recycling. One graduate, Jai, designed a full-length coat with an integrated disassembly and reconstruction system based on a take-back modular business model. Customers send back worn garments, which are then repurposed by reusing panels for new garments. Jai’s work was informed by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation butterfly diagram, applying circular economy principles to garment design. CLO3D was critical in demonstrating to factories and customers how garments can be disassembled and remade, addressing common visualization challenges. Jai also reimagined the conventional production and sales phases by integrating digital prototyping, emphasizing bespoke, on-demand manufacturing. This project investigated body scanning and avatar editing to ensure custom fit. Accurate avatar creation is crucial because up to 30% of high street garments fail to sell or are returned due to poor fit. Students combine body scans, imported object files, and conventional tailoring measurements to improve avatar accuracy, addressing body diversity including curvier shapes. CLO3D’s avatar editor has some limitations (e.g., lack of cup size variations), but remains a powerful tool for inclusive design. Jai merged body scan data and object files with avatars to test garments digitally before physical production, ensuring precision for custom pieces like trousers.

chunks.content: Accurate avatar creation is crucial because up to 30% of high street garments fail to sell or are returned due to poor fit. Students combine body scans, imported object files, and conventional tailoring measurements to improve avatar accuracy, addressing body diversity including curvier shapes. CLO3D’s avatar editor has some limitations (e.g., lack of cup size variations), but remains a powerful tool for inclusive design. Jai merged body scan data and object files with avatars to test garments digitally before physical production, ensuring precision for custom pieces like trousers. --- ## Digital to Physical Workflow and Pattern Development in CLO3D This section details the hybrid digital-physical workflow taught in the course, focusing on pattern creation, fitting, and amendments using CLO3D. Students learn to create and modify patterns digitally in CLO3D, using both 2D and 3D views simultaneously. Amendments can be made on 3D digital garments and reflected directly in 2D patterns, or vice versa, streamlining the traditional physical sample adjustment process. An example is given of a student, Yingxi, who optimized fabric usage by improving lay plans in CLO3D, reducing fabric waste from 2.5 meters to 2 meters. The lay plans, BOM (Bill of Materials), and other data are exported and integrated into ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) software such as Zedonk, demonstrating connection to real-world production management systems. The course emphasizes ERP over PLM (Product Lifecycle Management) at this scale for practicality. In physical-to-digital accuracy challenges, a student’s digital parka pattern showed discrepancies with the physical garment, such as a smaller hood in the digital version. These issues highlighted the importance of accurate digital material physics and precise pattern cutting in CLO3D, especially in the early stages of the course adoption. --- ## Advanced Digital Prototyping: Integration of CLO3D with Other Technologies This section covers the integration of CLO3D with other digital tools and emerging technologies for advanced fashion design and digital garment presentation. One notable project by Yaoyao involved reverse engineering garments from the designer duo Marknell’s Spring/Summer 2022 collection and creating 3D filters for a phone app using Snapchat. This enabled consumers to virtually try on garments before manufacturing, supporting production on demand. The workflow included importing designer patterns and avatar meshes into CLO3D’s avatar editor, creating digital garments, exporting to Mixamo for animation rigging, and finally integrating into Lens Studio for AR filters. This demonstrates CLO3D’s flexibility and interoperability within wider digital workflows rather than being an isolated tool. Students explore diverse interests ranging from visual media to motion capture (mocap). For example, Yiran Shan recreated Song Dynasty historical costumes using CLO3D and Unity3D, combining fashion design with cultural heritage and 3D technology. This project required understanding physical fabric properties and selecting accurate digital fabric simulations. Yiran’s project also included motion capture to animate avatars, illustrating how CLO3D supports both historical accuracy and digital animation workflows relevant to fashion and cultural projects.

chunks.content: This demonstrates CLO3D’s flexibility and interoperability within wider digital workflows rather than being an isolated tool. Students explore diverse interests ranging from visual media to motion capture (mocap). For example, Yiran Shan recreated Song Dynasty historical costumes using CLO3D and Unity3D, combining fashion design with cultural heritage and 3D technology. This project required understanding physical fabric properties and selecting accurate digital fabric simulations. Yiran’s project also included motion capture to animate avatars, illustrating how CLO3D supports both historical accuracy and digital animation workflows relevant to fashion and cultural projects. --- ## Industry 4.0 and Sustainable Bespoke Tailoring Platform This section describes Shenshan’s "Pocket Mobile Tailor" project, a platform concept that integrates emerging technologies with bespoke tailoring to promote sustainable, cost-effective fashion in Industry 4.0. The platform allows customers to register as avatars for virtual fittings. Two options exist: selecting default avatars or generating bespoke avatars via AI from two body photos. This supports remote bespoke design and personalized communication between customer and designer. Designers create sketches and virtual garments, communicating continuously through a text interface, allowing flexible, iterative design adjustments. Virtual garment approval can be done via 3D models, augmented reality (AR), or video. The platform supports real-time price estimation linked to design decisions, with customers paying a deposit before design work and final payment upon physical garment delivery. Customer feedback feeds into community ratings, helping designers attract new clients and enabling customers to become influencers. This fosters an active, creative ecosystem for independent designers, freelancers, fashion enthusiasts, and small manufacturers. The project exemplifies sustainable development in fashion by reducing physical sampling waste and enabling digital-to-physical workflows aligned with Industry 4.0 principles. --- # Summary of Key Technologies and Methods - **CLO3D**: Central tool for digital garment prototyping, pattern making, avatar editing, and virtual samples. - **OBJ files**: Used for sending detailed digital garment files to factories for inspection and production. - **Digital and Physical Construction**: Understanding particle distance and layering is critical to digital sewing accuracy. - **Body Scanning & Avatar Editing**: Combined with imported object files to create accurate and diverse avatars addressing fit and inclusivity. - **ERP Systems (e.g., Zedonk)**: Integration of BOM and production data from CLO3D for small-scale product management. - **Interoperability**: Exporting CLO3D garments and avatars into Mixamo for animation, Lens Studio for AR filters, and Unity3D for advanced visualization. - **Sustainability Focus**: Circular fashion business models, digital twins to reduce sampling waste, modular garments, and Industry 4.0 platforms. - **Motion Capture**: Used to animate avatars and simulate garment movement realistically. - **Digital Bespoke Platform**: AI-generated avatars, virtual fittings, real-time pricing, and community engagement supporting remote, sustainable bespoke tailoring. This structured approach equips students with practical skills bridging digital design and physical garment production while embedding sustainability and innovation at the core of fashion education.

Jai’s work was informed by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation butterfly diagram, applying circular economy principles to garment design. CLO3D was critical in demonstrating to factories and customers how garments can be disassembled and remade, addressing common visualization challenges. Jai also reimagined the conventional production and sales phases by integrating digital prototyping, emphasizing bespoke, on-demand manufacturing. This project investigated body scanning and avatar editing to ensure custom fit. Accurate avatar creation is crucial because up to 30% of high street garments fail to sell or are returned due to poor fit. Students combine body scans, imported object files, and conventional tailoring measurements to improve avatar accuracy, addressing body diversity including curvier shapes. CLO3D’s avatar editor has some limitations (e.g., lack of cup size variations), but remains a powerful tool for inclusive design. Jai merged body scan data and object files with avatars to test garments digitally before physical production, ensuring precision for custom pieces like trousers. --- ## Digital to Physical Workflow and Pattern Development in CLO3D This section details the hybrid digital-physical workflow taught in the course, focusing on pattern creation, fitting, and amendments using CLO3D. Students learn to create and modify patterns digitally in CLO3D, using both 2D and 3D views simultaneously. Amendments can be made on 3D digital garments and reflected directly in 2D patterns, or vice versa, streamlining the traditional physical sample adjustment process. An example is given of a student, Yingxi, who optimized fabric usage by improving lay plans in CLO3D, reducing fabric waste from 2.5 meters to 2 meters. The lay plans, BOM (Bill of Materials), and other data are exported and integrated into ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) software such as Zedonk, demonstrating connection to real-world production management systems. The course emphasizes ERP over PLM (Product Lifecycle Management) at this scale for practicality. In physical-to-digital accuracy challenges, a student’s digital parka pattern showed discrepancies with the physical garment, such as a smaller hood in the digital version. These issues highlighted the importance of accurate digital material physics and precise pattern cutting in CLO3D, especially in the early stages of the course adoption. --- ## Advanced Digital Prototyping: Integration of CLO3D with Other Technologies This section covers the integration of CLO3D with other digital tools and emerging technologies for advanced fashion design and digital garment presentation. One notable project by Yaoyao involved reverse engineering garments from the designer duo Marknell’s Spring/Summer 2022 collection and creating 3D filters for a phone app using Snapchat. This enabled consumers to virtually try on garments before manufacturing, supporting production on demand. The workflow included importing designer patterns and avatar meshes into CLO3D’s avatar editor, creating digital garments, exporting to Mixamo for animation rigging, and finally integrating into Lens Studio for AR filters. This demonstrates CLO3D’s flexibility and interoperability within wider digital workflows rather than being an isolated tool. Students explore diverse interests ranging from visual media to motion capture (mocap). For example, Yiran Shan recreated Song Dynasty historical costumes using CLO3D and Unity3D, combining fashion design with cultural heritage and 3D technology. This project required understanding physical fabric properties and selecting accurate digital fabric simulations. Yiran’s project also included motion capture to animate avatars, illustrating how CLO3D supports both historical accuracy and digital animation workflows relevant to fashion and cultural projects. --- ## Industry 4.0 and Sustainable Bespoke Tailoring Platform This section describes Shenshan’s "Pocket Mobile Tailor" project, a platform concept that integrates emerging technologies with bespoke tailoring to promote sustainable, cost-effective fashion in Industry 4.0. The platform allows customers to register as avatars for virtual fittings. Two options exist: selecting default avatars or generating bespoke avatars via AI from two body photos. This supports remote bespoke design and personalized communication between customer and designer. Designers create sketches and virtual garments, communicating continuously through a text interface, allowing flexible, iterative design adjustments. Virtual garment approval can be done via 3D models, augmented reality (AR), or video. The platform supports real-time price estimation linked to design decisions, with customers paying a deposit before design work and final payment upon physical garment delivery. Customer feedback feeds into community ratings, helping designers attract new clients and enabling customers to become influencers. This fosters an active, creative ecosystem for independent designers, freelancers, fashion enthusiasts, and small manufacturers. The project exemplifies sustainable development in fashion by reducing physical sampling waste and enabling digital-to-physical workflows aligned with Industry 4.0 principles. --- # Summary of Key Technologies and Methods - **CLO3D**: Central tool for digital garment prototyping, pattern making, avatar editing, and virtual samples. - **OBJ files**: Used for sending detailed digital garment files to factories for inspection and production. - **Digital and Physical Construction**: Understanding particle distance and layering is critical to digital sewing accuracy. - **Body Scanning & Avatar Editing**: Combined with imported object files to create accurate and diverse avatars addressing fit and inclusivity. - **ERP Systems (e.g., Zedonk)**: Integration of BOM and production data from CLO3D for small-scale product management. - **Interoperability**: Exporting CLO3D garments and avatars into Mixamo for animation, Lens Studio for AR filters, and Unity3D for advanced visualization. - **Sustainability Focus**: Circular fashion business models, digital twins to reduce sampling waste, modular garments, and Industry 4.0 platforms. - **Motion Capture**: Used to animate avatars and simulate garment movement realistically. - **Digital Bespoke Platform**: AI-generated avatars, virtual fittings, real-time pricing, and community engagement supporting remote, sustainable bespoke tailoring. This structured approach equips students with practical skills bridging digital design and physical garment production while embedding sustainability and innovation at the core of fashion education.
